title: Agent Bottlenecks Aren't in Context, but in Memory's Write, Change, Recall, Forget
dek: Uber burning through its token budget in 13 weeks proves stuffing context is wrong; MongoDB points to memory as the performance bottleneck—write, change, recall, forget—and suggests starting with employee use cases and human-in-the-loop.
why: This episode clears hurdles for Agent engineers: how to set chunk size, the 100k vector threshold, who writes and deletes memory; less valuable for those only interested in model progress.
who: Engineers building Agent/RAG applications, technical leads choosing data stacks for enterprises, investors tracking embedding models and vector databases.
skip: The first 30 minutes lean product-promotional; start at 16:38; around 31:51 is a feature release, can fast-forward.

points.h: Database schemas follow the scarcest resource
points.body: Pete dates the relational model to E.F. Codd's 1970 paper: when storage was priciest, normalized tables were rational. By MongoDB's 2007 birth, the scarce resource had become time, so the document model deliberately denormalizes, using JSON/BSON to cut disk reads. He also corrects a repeated misreading: MongoDB isn't 'schemaless' but 'schema-flexible'—the same collection can hold documents of different shapes, letting schema evolve with the product. This design logic shows database schemas should follow whatever resource is scarcest at the time.

points.h: Stuffing context with data degrades quality
points.body: Uber burning through its 2026 token budget in 13 weeks is treated as a failed token-maxing strategy. Cost is only half the problem; quality drops too: research shows the first and last few thousand tokens of a window matter most, the middle is mostly noise. This pushes the industry toward 'classified memory'—selecting only the few terms relevant to the current agent loop each turn, rather than replaying all history. The key isn't saving money but that attention decay inside the context makes selective retrieval a performance issue.

points.h: AI features grow from where customers already hurt
points.body: MongoDB's search capabilities grew layer by layer from customer pain: lexical search in 2020 because many were building their own Lucene; then vector search because vectors are essentially float arrays, naturally a document field; then combining lexical, vector, and metadata pre-filtering into one hybrid search. In 2025 they acquired Voyage AI to bring embedding models in-house, forming a 'better together' offering. This sequence itself shows infrastructure companies touching AI typically start from where customers already hurt, not by buying models first and inventing use cases.

points.h: Chunk size tuning should be delegated to the model
points.body: RAG's first nagging problem is chunk size: too small, context insufficient and retrieval quality poor; too large, storage grows and precision drops, forcing manual trial-and-error. Voyage's 'contextual chunking' sends the sentence and extra context as two strings into the model, which automatically decides the optimal chunk size and returns a single vector. This achieves near-full-context retrieval quality with very small chunks and lower storage cost, now in its fourth version. It's a concrete example of moving the engineer's iterative tuning into model weights.

points.h: Embedding models aren't commoditized; selection drives hallucinations
points.body: Pete gives two selection thresholds: on scale, you really start to feel pain around 100k vectors; on quality, Voyage leads Hugging Face's RTEB benchmark, improving retrieval by up to 14% over other embedding models—a gap that can directly manifest as hallucinations. He also warns embedding models aren't commoditized—Anthropic doesn't build its own embedding model, so his advice is to use Voyage directly. For many teams, embedding model selection has long been undervalued; this segment puts it back at the center of performance and hallucinations.

points.h: Memory has a half-life and must be actively retired
points.body: Why is memory hard? Pete's analogy: the industry has built databases for sixty years, but agents for about eighteen months. Long-term context strategy is no longer stuffing the whole conversation back; it's recalling best context at query time and writing new facts back to memory after answering; enterprise systems use RBAC to control memory sharing and isolation. He sums up the loop with a colleague's phrase: Write, change, recall, forget. Memory has a half-life—recent information matters more than weeks or months old. This means agent memory must be a first-class citizen, with intentional writing, updating, and retiring.

points.h: First enterprise AI wave lands on employees, not customers
points.body: Most Fortune 500 companies Pete talks to are doing employee-facing use cases with humans in the loop. Two reasons: ROI is easier to calculate—these roles already have KPIs—and data security consequences are lighter; employee data leaks are easier to handle than customer data. Conversely, fully autonomous customer-facing agents are a worse risk-reward bet right now. This segment gives a coordinate for enterprise AI budget judgments: the first wave is more likely in internal efficiency tools than in robots making final decisions for customers.

points.h: Most sophisticated customers aren't in the US but in Mexico City and São Paulo
points.body: Pete met this year's most sophisticated customers in Mexico City and São Paulo, and these customers typically assume US competitors are more advanced. He says he sees the opposite. He attributes this to the spread of hyperscale data centers and AI services, making geography less important than in the cloud era and leveling global access to technology. This observation suggests country labels are increasingly unreliable for judging whether a company can use cutting-edge AI.
